meta.title: Section I — Power and Authority in the Modern World
meta.range: 1919–1946 · Germany (Weimar & Nazi Germany), with the Survey and comparative dictatorships · Source-based, 25 marks, ~45 min

boxes.label: Examinable
boxes.bodyHtml: All syllabus content — the WWI peace treaties, the conditions for the rise of dictatorships, the collapse of Weimar democracy, Hitler's rise, Nazi consolidation of power, the Nazi state and its impact on German society to 1939, and the search for peace and security to 1946.

boxes.label: Format reminder
boxes.bodyHtml: 3–4 short answers, at least one worth 10–15 marks. Expect one or two written or visual sources to open the section.

summary.note: Every official syllabus dot point for this topic is listed below, grouped as the syllabus itself groups them.

groups.title: Survey — The Peace Treaties & Postwar Conditions
points: Treaty of Versailles (28 June 1919): imposed the "war guilt" clause (Article 231), fixed reparations at 132 billion gold marks (1921), stripped Germany of roughly 13% of its territory and all colonies, and capped the army at 100,000 men with no air force, tanks or submarines.

Related peace treaties: St Germain (Austria), Trianon (Hungary), Neuilly (Bulgaria) and Sèvres/Lausanne (Ottoman Empire) redrew Central and Eastern Europe and created new states, including Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia.
Postwar resentment: the "Diktat" (dictated peace) was resented across the German political spectrum, fuelling nationalist and revisionist movements later exploited by the Nazis.

groups.title: The Rise of Dictatorships After World War I
points: Economic dislocation: war debts, hyperinflation (Germany, 1923) and the Great Depression from 1929 undermined faith in parliamentary democracy across Europe.
Fear of communism: the Bolshevik Revolution (1917) pushed conservative elites and the middle class toward authoritarian alternatives seen as a bulwark against the political left.
Weakness of new democracies: proportional representation produced unstable coalition governments (e.g. Weimar Germany), while states like Italy lacked deep democratic traditions to begin with.

Common features of emerging dictatorships: rejection of liberal-democratic values, loyalty to the state/leader placed above individual rights, propaganda and paramilitary violence, and charismatic leadership offering simple solutions and scapegoats.

Comparative examples: Russia (Bolshevik one-party state from 1917); Italy (Mussolini's March on Rome, Oct 1922, dictatorship consolidated by 1925–26); Japan (the military progressively dominating civilian government through the 1930s).

groups.title: The Weimar Republic, 1919–1929
points: Foundation: proclaimed 9 November 1918 amid the Kaiser's abdication; the Weimar Constitution (Aug 1919) established a president with Article 48 emergency powers, a Reichstag elected by proportional representation, and a Chancellor-led government.

Early crises: the Spartacist Uprising (Jan 1919, crushed by Freikorps), the Kapp Putsch (1920), the French/Belgian occupation of the Ruhr (1923) and the resulting hyperinflation, in which the mark became worthless by November 1923.
Hitler's failed Beer Hall Putsch (8–9 Nov 1923) led to his imprisonment, during which he wrote Mein Kampf.

The "Golden Years", 1924–1929 under Stresemann: the Rentenmark stabilised the currency, the Dawes Plan (1924) and Young Plan (1929) rescheduled reparations, and the Locarno Treaties (1925) plus League of Nations membership (1926) restored international standing.

groups.title: Hitler's Rise to Power, 1919–1933
points: NSDAP origins: Hitler joined the German Workers' Party in 1919 and became leader by 1921; the 25-Point Programme combined nationalism, antisemitism and anti-Versailles revisionism.
The "legal" strategy: after the failed 1923 Putsch, Hitler pursued power through elections rather than force.
Impact of the Great Depression: unemployment reached around 6 million by 1932; Nazi Reichstag seats rose from 12 (1928) to 230 (July 1932).
Appointment as Chancellor: Hitler was appointed Chancellor by President Hindenburg on 30 January 1933, in a backroom deal with conservative elites who believed they could control him.

groups.title: Nazi Consolidation of Power, 1933–1934
points: Reichstag Fire (27 Feb 1933) was used to justify the Reichstag Fire Decree, suspending civil liberties.
Enabling Act (23 March 1933) allowed Hitler's cabinet to pass laws without Reichstag approval, ending Weimar democracy in practice.
Gleichschaltung ("coordination"): trade unions banned and other political parties dissolved; Germany was a one-party state by July 1933.
Night of the Long Knives (30 June – 2 July 1934): the SA leadership under Röhm was purged to appease the army and secure Hitler's position.
Death of Hindenburg (2 Aug 1934) allowed Hitler to merge the presidency and chancellorship as Führer; the army swore a personal oath of allegiance to him.

groups.title: The Nazi State: Ideology, Control & Society
points: Core ideology: Volksgemeinschaft ("people's community"), Führerprinzip (absolute hierarchical authority), racial theory placing "Aryans" atop a constructed racial hierarchy, and Lebensraum ("living space") ambitions in the east.

Instruments of control: the Gestapo relied less on its own manpower than on a culture of public denunciation; the SS under Himmler grew from Hitler's bodyguard into a state within the state, with its own courts, army units and factories by the 1940s; concentration camps (Dachau, Sachsenhausen and Buchenwald all opened 1933–37) held over 200,000 people between 1934 and 1939, mostly political prisoners and "socially deviant" groups.

Propaganda and censorship: Goebbels' Ministry of Propaganda controlled press (the state owned an estimated 82% of newspapers by 1944), radio (cheap state-subsidised sets that could only receive German stations) and film (e.g. Triumph of the Will, Jud Süss), alongside book-burning and the Reich Chamber of Culture, which barred Jewish artists outright.

Antisemitic legislation: boycotts of Jewish businesses (1933), exclusion from the civil service and universities, the Nuremberg Laws (Sept 1935) stripping Jews of citizenship and banning intermarriage, and Kristallnacht (9–10 Nov 1938) — over 400 pieces of anti-Jewish legislation were passed between 1933 and 1939.

The Holocaust: from the September 1939 invasion of Poland, mobile killing squads carried out mass shootings; Jews were confined to overcrowded ghettos (Warsaw held around 446,000 people in roughly 400 hectares by early 1941); from late 1941 the regime built dedicated death camps under Operation Reinhard — Chelmno (opened Dec 1941) was first, followed by Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka in 1942 — while Auschwitz-Birkenau's gas chambers could kill up to 1,200 people at a time. An estimated six million Jews were murdered, roughly two-thirds of Europe's 1939 Jewish population; Roma and Sinti, disabled Germans, and other targeted groups were also killed in the hundreds of thousands.
Economic policy: Schacht's work-creation schemes and rearmament cut unemployment sharply by the mid-1930s; the Four Year Plan (1936, under Göring) prioritised military self-sufficiency ahead of war.

Society and culture: the Hitler Youth (compulsory for boys 10–18 from 1936, around 8 million members by 1939) and League of German Girls indoctrinated the young both in and out of school; "degenerate art" and jazz were banned in favour of "heroic" Aryan realism; churches faced varying pressure and co-option, most explicitly through the 1933 Reich Concordat with the Catholic Church.

groups.title: Prominent Individuals in the Nazi State
points: Hitler did not rule alone: power was distributed among a small circle of lieutenants who built and ran the regime's key institutions, often in overlapping and competing jurisdictions that Hitler himself did little to resolve.

Joseph Goebbels — Reich Minister of Propaganda and Enlightenment from 1933, controlling press, radio, film, theatre and the arts; historians credit him with constructing the "Hitler myth" that presented Hitler as both extraordinary and humble. He orchestrated Kristallnacht, remained with Hitler in the Berlin bunker to the end, and killed his six children before he and his wife took their own lives in May 1945.

Hermann Göring — WWI flying ace and early Party member who became President of the Reichstag in 1932; he built up the Gestapo before handing it to Himmler, led the Luftwaffe, and took over the Four Year Plan from Schacht in 1937. Widely seen as the most publicly popular Nazi leader, he was convicted at Nuremberg and took poison the night before his scheduled execution (Oct 1946).

Heinrich Himmler — Head of the SS from 1929, central to purging the SA in the Night of the Long Knives, and from 1934 built control over the Gestapo and criminal police into one of the most powerful roles in the regime. As Reich Interior Minister from 1943 he oversaw the Final Solution and the forced-labour system; captured by the Allies, he took his own life in custody on 23 May 1945.

Albert Speer — an architect who joined the Party in 1931 and designed Nazi monuments including the Nuremberg rally grounds; as Minister of Armaments and Munitions from 1942 he is credited with dramatically increasing German war production, achieved partly through the use of prisoners of war and slave labour. At Nuremberg he expressed remorse while denying direct knowledge of the extermination of the Jews, served 20 years at Spandau Prison, and died in 1981.

groups.title: Opposition and Resistance to the Nazi Regime
points: Historians distinguish opposition (acts openly defying the regime, e.g. listening to foreign radio, hiding Jewish people, refusing the Hitler salute) from resistance (organised attempts to overthrow the regime) — opposition was far more common than organised resistance, and even resistance movements had little practical impact given the scale of the police state.

Political undergrounds: the banned KPD ran underground cells distributing literature and organising illegal strikes, activity that increased after Germany invaded the USSR in 1941; the "Red Orchestra" network passed intelligence on German war plans to Moscow; the exiled SPD leadership smuggled in banned literature and encouraged industrial sabotage.

Youth opposition: "Swing" groups of middle-class youth held illicit parties and adopted British/American fashion in defiance of Nazi culture; the Edelweiss Pirates refused Hitler Youth membership and clashed physically with its patrols — a December 1942 crackdown broke up 28 groups, arresting 700 members, some of whom were publicly hanged.

Church opposition: Pastor Martin Niemöller founded the dissident Confessing Church against the Nazified Protestant Church; he was imprisoned and around 800 of its members were sent to concentration camps. The Catholic Church protested restrictions on its schools and youth groups despite the 1933 Concordat, with limited success.

Elite and military resistance: the Kreisau Circle, an informal network of aristocrats and officials opposed to Hitler, mostly debated rather than acted; the more organised Beck–Goerdeler group (army chief of staff Ludwig Beck and Leipzig mayor Carl Goerdeler) built contacts across the police, foreign office and intelligence services and passed warnings to Britain, though notably sought an authoritarian successor state rather than a return to democracy.

Assassination attempts: from 1943 army resistance shifted toward assassinating Hitler directly; of six known attempts only two bombs actually detonated, both failing to kill him. The most significant, the 20 July 1944 July Plot (Operation Valkyrie), aimed to kill Hitler and seize government control to negotiate peace — it failed, and its conspirators were executed.

groups.title: The Search for Peace and Security, 1919–1946
points: The League of Nations: founded 1919 to preserve peace through collective security and arbitration; weakened structurally by the absence of the USA, a unanimity rule, and no standing military force.

League successes and failures: successes at the Aaland Islands (1921) and Upper Silesia (1921) contrast with failures over Japan's invasion of Manchuria (1931) and Italy's invasion of Abyssinia (1935).

German ambitions: reversing Versailles, open rearmament (1935), remilitarising the Rhineland (1936), and pursuing Lebensraum through the Anschluss with Austria (1938) and annexation of the Sudetenland (1938).
Japanese ambitions in the Asia-Pacific: resource security and regional dominance drove the invasion of Manchuria (1931) and full-scale war with China from 1937.

Formation of the United Nations: the Atlantic Charter (1941) and Dumbarton Oaks proposals (1944) shaped a new organisation; the UN Charter was signed by 50 founding members in San Francisco on 26 June 1945, creating a Security Council with binding enforcement power to address the League's key weakness.

sources.tag: Source A — Political poster, NSDAP election campaign, 1932 (described)
sources.bodyHtml: A large stylised image of Adolf Hitler's head and shoulders dominates the poster, rendered in stark red and black. Behind him, faceless lines of marching men stretch to the horizon, suggesting mass unity. A single bold slogan beneath the image promises strong, decisive national leadership and an end to the divisions of party politics.

sources.tag: Source B — Adapted historian's viewpoint (composite, for practice use)
sources.bodyHtml: "The Weimar Republic did not fall to Nazism so much as it was abandoned by a public exhausted by economic hardship, street violence and a decade of unstable coalition government. Hitler did not need to convert Germans to Nazi ideology in 1932 — he needed only to appear more competent than the alternatives."

sources.tag: Source C — Luise Solmitz, German schoolteacher, diary entry describing an SA torchlight procession, early 1930s
sources.bodyHtml: "20,000 brownshirts followed one another like waves in the sea, their faces shone with enthusiasm... They sang The Republic is shit... They sang of the blood of the Jews which would squirt from their knives."

groups.title: Survey — WWI Peace Treaties & the Rise of Dictatorships

questions.questionHtml: Explain how the terms of the Treaty of Versailles contributed to political instability in postwar Germany.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Territorial and military terms: Germany lost c. 13% of its territory including Alsace-Lorraine and all overseas colonies; the army was capped at 100,000 men with no air force, tanks or submarines, and the Rhineland was demilitarised — read as a humiliation of national sovereignty.
  • War guilt and reparations: Article 231 assigned Germany sole blame for the war; the 1921 London Schedule of Payments fixed reparations at 132 billion gold marks, a bill widely seen as economically crippling before a single payment was made.
  • Political fallout: the treaty was signed by the new civilian government, not the Kaiser's army command — feeding the "stab-in-the-back" (Dolchstoss) myth that politicians, not soldiers, had betrayed Germany, a grievance right-wing parties exploited for the next decade.

questions.questionHtml: Assess the conditions across postwar Europe that allowed dictatorships to emerge in the 1920s and 1930s, with reference to TWO countries other than Germany.
questions.planHtml:
Thesis

Dictatorship did not emerge from any single cause repeated across Europe and Asia, but from a common structural pattern: newly formed or fragile parliamentary systems that met an economic or military crisis they lacked the legitimacy and institutional depth to survive. Russia, Italy and Japan reached dictatorship by different ideological routes, but each collapse followed that same underlying logic.

Point 1 — Russia

Tsarist autocracy was never a parliamentary democracy to begin with, but its collapse establishes the pattern the other two cases follow: a regime destroyed by the strain of total war rather than by the strength of its opposition. Russia suffered an estimated 1.7 million military deaths by 1917, and the war's continuation under the Provisional Government — rather than any positive Bolshevik programme — is what destroyed its authority. That the Bolsheviks were able to seize power in Petrograd on 24–25 October 1917 with only a handful of casualties is itself evidence of how little institutional resistance remained; there was no functioning state left to defend, only one waiting to be claimed.

Point 2 — Italy

Italy shows the same vacuum filled by ideology rather than force. The "mutilated victory" grievance after WWI combined with the biennio rosso factory occupations of 1919–20 to convince Italy's industrialists and landowners that liberal government could no longer guarantee social order. This elite fear, not popular enthusiasm, is the decisive factor: Mussolini's March on Rome in October 1922 involved perhaps 30,000 Blackshirts against a state that could still have resisted militarily, yet King Victor Emmanuel III chose to appoint him Prime Minister rather than risk civil conflict. The dictatorship was handed over, not seized.

Point 3 — Japan

Japan demonstrates that the same pattern did not require an economic collapse as severe as Germany's to produce authoritarian drift — only a parliamentary system too weak to control its own military. The Depression halved Japan's raw silk export earnings by the early 1930s, deepening rural hardship and discrediting civilian politicians who could offer no solution. Decisively, the military's invasion of Manchuria in September 1931 proceeded without civilian government authorisation and was retrospectively endorsed rather than punished — proof that institutional power had already shifted before any formal change of government occurred.

Judgement

What unites these three cases is not ideology but sequence: in each, an economic or military crisis exposed a democratic system without deep roots, and the resulting vacuum was filled by whichever organised force — Bolshevik, Fascist, or military — was disciplined enough to act while its rivals hesitated. Dictatorship, in other words, was less imposed than allowed to happen.

questions.questionHtml: What message does Source A convey about Hitler's proposed leadership of Germany?
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include
  • Visual feature 1: Hitler's dominant, larger-than-life portrait → suggests strong, singular leadership.
  • Visual feature 2: uniform lines of marching men → suggests national unity and mass discipline behind him.
  • Link the slogan to a promise of decisive government, contrasted implicitly with coalition instability.
Note
2-mark "identify" questions need no outside knowledge — one sentence per feature is enough.

questions.questionHtml: Using Source A, Source B and your own knowledge, assess the reasons for growing public support for the Nazi Party by 1932.
questions.planHtml:
Thesis

The sources present Nazi support as a matter of image and exhaustion — a party that simply looked more competent than its exhausted rivals. This is accurate as far as it goes, but it understates the extent to which that "image" was manufactured out of a specific, quantifiable economic collapse and then converted into power by elite miscalculation rather than popular mandate.

Point 1 — what the sources show

Both sources frame Nazi appeal in terms of order over division rather than ideological persuasion. Source A constructs this visually — Hitler's dominant portrait against disciplined, uniform ranks of marching men — while Source B makes the same claim explicitly, attributing Nazi success to voter exhaustion with "a decade of unstable coalition government" rather than any genuine conversion to Nazi ideology. Taken together, the sources argue that Germans were choosing competence, not doctrine.

Point 2 — economic collapse (own knowledge)

What the sources don't explain is why "competence" suddenly became so urgent a demand, and the answer is a specific, dateable economic collapse. Unemployment reached roughly 6 million — around 30% of the workforce — by early 1932, and Chancellor Brüning's deflationary response of spending cuts and tax rises deepened rather than eased the crisis, destroying his government's credibility so completely that the "Grand Coalition" collapsed in March 1930. The image Source A sells only had a market because this collapse had already discredited every alternative.

Point 3 — political calculation (own knowledge)

The final and most decisive factor lies outside the sources entirely: elite fear of the political left. The KPD won nearly 17% of the vote in November 1932, close behind the Nazis, and this genuinely alarmed industrialists and landowners far more than Nazi rhetoric did. It was this calculation, not electoral arithmetic, that led Papen and Hindenburg's inner circle to install Hitler as Chancellor on 30 January 1933, in the belief he could be "boxed in" by conservative ministers around him.

Judgement

The sources' "positive appeal" argument is not wrong, but it is incomplete: a party whose vote share peaked at 37.3% in July 1932 — never a majority — was ultimately delivered power by a small circle of conservative elites reacting to economic crisis and fear of communism, not by a nation persuaded of Nazi ideology.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the political and economic weaknesses of the Weimar Republic in the years up to 1923.
questions.planHtml:
Structure & evidence
  1. Constitutional weaknesses: proportional representation split the vote across many small parties, producing no single-party majority in any Reichstag of the period; Article 48 allowed rule by emergency decree, a power later abused.
  2. Legitimacy problem: the "stab-in-the-back" myth and resentment over Versailles saw the new government branded the "November Criminals" for signing the armistice of 11 November 1918.
  3. Early violent challenges: the Spartacist Uprising (January 1919), crushed by Freikorps units who killed leaders Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, and the Kapp Putsch (March 1920), defeated only by a general strike — both show a republic unable to secure loyalty from left or right.
  4. Economic collapse: after France occupied the Ruhr in January 1923 over missed reparations payments, hyperinflation spiralled until the exchange rate reached over 4 trillion marks to the US dollar by November 1923, wiping out savings and pensions.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the reasons for the recovery of the Weimar Republic under Stresemann, 1924–1929.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Currency stabilised via the temporary Rentenmark (Nov 1923), replaced by the Reichsmark in 1924, ending hyperinflation almost overnight.
  • The Dawes Plan (1924) restructured reparations and brought an initial $200 million US loan; the Young Plan (1929) further reduced the total reparations bill to 112 billion gold marks payable over 59 years.
  • The Locarno Treaties (1925) and League of Nations membership (1926) restored international respectability and diplomatic standing.
  • Caveat: recovery was shallow — by 1928 Germany relied on short-term US loans exceeding 25 billion marks since 1924, leaving the economy exposed once US capital was withdrawn after 1929.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the significance of the Munich Putsch (1923) for the later development of the Nazi Party.
questions.planHtml:
Structure & evidence
  1. The event: the failed 8–9 November 1923 attempt to seize power in a Munich beer hall, inspired partly by Mussolini's March on Rome, collapsed when police fired on the marchers, killing 16 Nazis and 4 police.
  2. Immediate consequence: Hitler's trial gave him a national stage; he was sentenced to 5 years but served only 9 months in Landsberg Prison.
  3. Strategic shift: in prison Hitler wrote Mein Kampf (dictated 1924) and concluded the Party must pursue power through legal, electoral means rather than force — shaping NSDAP strategy for the rest of the 1920s.

questions.questionHtml: Assess the reasons for the growth in support for the Nazi Party between 1929 and 1933.
questions.planHtml:
Thesis

The Depression was a necessary but not sufficient cause of Nazi power: it created the electoral conditions for growth, but it was Nazi organisational capacity and, ultimately, elite miscalculation — not popular majority support — that converted that growth into government. The Nazis never won a majority of the vote; they were handed power by people who believed they could control them.

Point 1 — economic crisis

The correlation between economic collapse and Nazi electoral growth is close to exact. After the Wall Street Crash of October 1929, American loans underpinning the German economy were recalled, and unemployment climbed from 1.3 million in 1929 to roughly 6 million by early 1932. NSDAP vote share tracked this collapse almost step for step: 2.6% in 1928, 18.3% by September 1930, and 37.3% by July 1932 — a fifteen-fold increase over four years of deepening crisis.

Point 2 — Nazi organisation and campaigning

Crisis alone does not explain why voters moved specifically to the Nazis rather than other opposition parties; organisational capacity does. The SA numbered around 400,000 members by 1932, projecting an image of physical order at rallies that contrasted with a paralysed parliamentary system, while Hitler's 1932 "Flight over Germany" campaign used aircraft to reach over 20 cities in weeks — a scale and speed of campaigning no rival party could match.

Point 3 — elite miscalculation

Crucially, none of this delivered a majority: the Nazi vote actually fell to 33.1% in the November 1932 election, and support looked to be plateauing. Power came instead from a deliberate elite decision — Papen and Hindenburg's circle appointed Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933 with only three Nazis in an eleven-seat cabinet, on the calculation, in Papen's own words, that they had "hired" him and could box him in.

Judgement

Structural economic crisis created the electoral opportunity, but it was a specific, avoidable political decision in January 1933 — not an outright popular mandate — that finally delivered power. The rise of the Nazi Party was not inevitable; it required conservative elites to gamble wrongly at exactly the right moment.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how Hitler used legal and extra-legal means to establish a dictatorship in Germany by August 1934.
questions.planHtml:
Structure & evidence
  1. Reichstag Fire, 27 February 1933: used to justify the Reichstag Fire Decree the next day, suspending civil liberties and enabling the arrest of thousands of communists.
  2. Enabling Act, 23 March 1933: passed 444 votes to 94 (only the SPD voted against; KPD deputies were already excluded) — allowed Hitler to legislate without the Reichstag, giving a legal veneer to dictatorship.
  3. Elimination of rivals: trade unions banned 2 May 1933; all other parties banned by the Law Against the Formation of New Parties, 14 July 1933 — creating a formal one-party state.
  4. Night of the Long Knives, 30 June – 2 July 1934: extra-legal purge killing an estimated 85–200 people, including SA leader Röhm, to win over the army; Hindenburg's death on 2 August 1934 let Hitler merge the Chancellor and President roles into Führer, with the army swearing a personal oath of loyalty to him.

questions.questionHtml: To what extent did the Nazi regime rely on terror rather than genuine popular support to maintain control over German society, 1933–1939?
questions.planHtml:
Introduction — Thesis

Terror and consent were not alternative explanations for Nazi control but sequential ones: terror was the mechanism that destroyed organised opposition in the regime's first eighteen months, while consent, built through economic recovery and propaganda, is what explains why that control held for the rest of the decade without needing to be constantly reasserted by force. To treat 1933–39 as a single, unchanging system of rule misses this shift.

Body Paragraph 1 — the terror apparatus

In its first phase, the regime relied overwhelmingly on coercion because organised alternatives to it still existed. The Gestapo, formed in 1933, worked less through its own manpower than through a culture of public denunciation that turned ordinary citizens into instruments of surveillance, while Dachau — the first concentration camp, opened March 1933 — initially held communists and socialists specifically, the two groups capable of mounting organised resistance. By 1939, an estimated 150,000–200,000 Germans had passed through such camps for political reasons, a scale sufficient to break the KPD and SPD as functioning organisations within the regime's first year.

Body Paragraph 2 — propaganda and the Führer cult

Once organised opposition was gone, propaganda did work terror could not — shaping belief rather than merely suppressing dissent. Goebbels' Ministry of Propaganda built an image of Hitler as a leader standing above ordinary party politics, reinforced through annual Nuremberg rallies that drew crowds estimated at over 700,000 by the late 1930s. By 1939, around 70% of German households owned a radio, many via the state-subsidised Volksempfänger, giving the regime direct, daily access into homes that no amount of policing could achieve on its own.

Body Paragraph 3 — genuine consent through recovery

Beneath the propaganda sat a material reality that made the message credible: unemployment fell from roughly 6 million in 1933 to under 1 million by 1938, driven by public works such as the autobahn network and by rearmament spending. Schemes like Strength Through Joy offered subsidised holidays to millions of workers who had never travelled before — a tangible improvement in daily life that terror alone could never have manufactured, and which gave most Germans, who were never themselves targeted by the Gestapo, a genuine stake in the regime's continuation.

Conclusion — Judgement

Terror explains how the regime survived its first year in power; consent explains why it did not need to rule by terror for the rest of the decade. By 1939, most Germans were not afraid of the regime so much as materially and ideologically invested in it — control had shifted from coercion to something closer to complicity.

questions.questionHtml: Assess the impact of Nazi economic policy, including the Four Year Plan, on ordinary Germans between 1933 and 1939.
questions.planHtml:
Thesis

Nazi economic policy achieved a real and rapid statistical recovery, but the headline figures conceal a deliberate redirection of that recovery toward military readiness rather than consumer welfare — the ordinary German experienced a job, not necessarily a better standard of living.

Point 1 — recovery measures

The most visible achievement was a genuine collapse in unemployment, driven by public works such as the autobahn network (begun 1933) and by rearmament spending, which together cut unemployment from around 6 million to under 1 million by 1938 — a recovery unmatched anywhere else in Depression-era Europe.

Point 2 — the Four Year Plan

That recovery was never intended as an end in itself. The Four Year Plan, launched in 1936 under Göring, explicitly targeted military and economic self-sufficiency (autarky) within four years, prioritising synthetic fuel and rubber production over consumer goods — a clear statement that the economy's purpose was war-readiness, not living standards.

Point 3 — impact on living standards

This priority had a direct cost for ordinary workers: real wages remained largely frozen at Depression-era levels even as working hours lengthened, and independent trade unions were replaced by the state-run German Labour Front from May 1933, removing any mechanism for workers to bargain for a larger share of the recovery. By 1939, military spending absorbed around one-quarter of GNP, crowding out consumer production even as unemployment fell.

Judgement

Headline unemployment statistics masked an economy increasingly geared to war readiness rather than consumer welfare — recovery was real, but its benefits were unevenly distributed and secured at the direct expense of worker bargaining power.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how the Nazi regime sought to control German youth, education and the churches.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Hitler Youth membership became compulsory for boys aged 10–18 under a December 1936 law; membership reached around 8 million by 1939, embedding Nazi ideology outside the classroom.
  • Curriculum changes introduced race science and biology as core subjects, alongside heavy emphasis on physical education and revised history teaching glorifying German military tradition.
  • The Reich Concordat with the Catholic Church (July 1933) traded away Church political involvement for continued religious freedom; Protestant churches faced pressure from the state-backed "German Christians" movement, with resistance from the Confessing Church led by figures such as Martin Niemöller.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the impact of Nazi racial policy on Jewish Germans in the years before 1939.
questions.planHtml:
Structure & evidence
  1. Early measures, 1933: a one-day national boycott of Jewish businesses (1 April 1933) and the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service (April 1933) excluded Jewish Germans from public employment.
  2. Nuremberg Laws, September 1935: the Reich Citizenship Law stripped Jewish Germans of citizenship; the Law for the Protection of German Blood banned marriage and sexual relations with "Aryans" — legalising segregation.
  3. Escalation — Kristallnacht, 9–10 November 1938: coordinated violence destroyed around 267 synagogues and 7,000 Jewish-owned businesses; at least 91 people were killed and around 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps.
  4. Effect: growing social, legal and economic exclusion drove roughly half of Germany's Jewish population to emigrate between 1933 and 1939, before the outbreak of war closed off most escape routes.
Historian's view — verified quote
"The road to Auschwitz was built by hate, but paved with indifference."Ian Kershaw, Popular Opinion and Political Dissent in the Third Reich: Bavaria 1933–45 (1983), p. 277
Useful for a concluding line: it lets you argue that everyday public apathy, not just official policy, allowed persecution to escalate unchecked through the 1930s.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the role and experience of women in Nazi Germany.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Official ideology of "Kinder, Küche, Kirche" (children, kitchen, church) encouraged women out of the paid workforce and into domestic/maternal roles; female civil servants and doctors were dismissed from 1933.
  • Marriage loans of up to 1,000 Reichsmarks were offered from 1933, with a quarter forgiven per child; the Mother's Cross award (instituted 1938) recognised women with four or more children.
  • Contradiction after 1936: rearmament labour shortages saw growing pressure for women to re-enter certain sectors of the workforce, undercutting the regime's own domestic ideology by the late 1930s.

groups.title: Prominent Individuals & Opposition to the Regime

questions.questionHtml: What does Source C reveal about the culture of the SA and its supporters in the years before 1933?
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include
  • The scale and discipline of the procession ("20,000 brownshirts... like waves in the sea") conveys mass, organised support rather than a fringe movement.
  • The genuine "enthusiasm" on display shows this was not coerced participation — ordinary Germans found real appeal in Nazi spectacle.
  • The explicit contempt for the Republic and violent antisemitism in the marching songs show the movement's aggression and racism were open and public, not hidden, well before the regime took power.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the roles played by TWO prominent individuals in establishing and maintaining the Nazi state.
questions.planHtml:
Structure & evidence
  1. Choose two distinct roles to show breadth — e.g. Goebbels (propaganda/ideology) and Himmler (terror/policing) cover different instruments of control.
  2. Goebbels: as Minister of Propaganda from 1933 he controlled press, radio and film, and is credited by historians with constructing the "Hitler myth"; he orchestrated Kristallnacht (Nov 1938) and remained loyal to the end, killing his family in the Berlin bunker in May 1945.
  3. Himmler: built the SS from Hitler's bodyguard into a parallel state apparatus with its own courts and army units, engineered the Night of the Long Knives (1934), and from 1943 as Interior Minister directed the Final Solution and forced-labour system before taking his own life in Allied custody.
  4. Link back: both examples show power in the Nazi state was distributed among competing lieutenants, not exercised by Hitler alone.

questions.questionHtml: Assess the effectiveness of opposition and resistance to the Nazi regime, 1933–1945.
questions.planHtml:
Thesis

Opposition to the Nazi regime was widespread but largely symbolic, while organised resistance capable of threatening the regime was rare, poorly coordinated, and ultimately unsuccessful — the police state's use of denunciation and terror made effective resistance almost impossible before the regime's military defeat.

Point 1 — everyday opposition

Everyday defiance was common but had negligible practical effect: youth groups such as the Edelweiss Pirates rejected Hitler Youth membership and clashed with its patrols, but a single December 1942 crackdown broke up 28 groups and arrested 700 members, some publicly hanged as a deterrent — showing how easily such opposition was contained.

Point 2 — political and religious resistance

More organised networks like the Communist underground and the Red Orchestra passed intelligence to Moscow, while Pastor Niemöller's Confessing Church resisted Nazification of Protestantism — but the Gestapo's reliance on public denunciation meant such networks were consistently infiltrated and broken, with around 800 Confessing Church members sent to concentration camps.

Point 3 — elite and military resistance

The most credible threat came from within the state itself: the Beck–Goerdeler network built contacts across the police and foreign office, and the army's 20 July 1944 July Plot came the closest of six known assassination attempts to succeeding — yet even this failed, and its leaders sought an authoritarian, not democratic, successor state.

Judgement

Across every category, opposition registered moral defiance rather than practical threat — the regime's terror apparatus and its penetration of everyday life through informants meant no resistance movement came close to overthrowing Hitler until Germany's military collapse made the question moot.

groups.title: The Search for Peace and Security in the World

questions.questionHtml: Explain the aims and structural weaknesses of the League of Nations as a mechanism for collective security in the interwar period.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Aim: prevent future war through collective security, arbitration and disarmament, established under the Treaty of Versailles with 42 founding members in 1920.
  • Structural weakness: no standing army and reliance on member states to enforce sanctions; the US Senate voted against joining in 1919–20, removing the world's largest economy from its authority.
  • Practical failure: unable to stop Japan's invasion of Manchuria (1931, Japan withdrew from the League in 1933) or Italy's invasion of Abyssinia (1935, sanctions excluded oil and Italy withdrew in 1937) — both aggressors faced condemnation but no meaningful cost.

questions.questionHtml: Compare the territorial and authoritarian ambitions of Germany and Japan in the years leading up to 1941, and assess the effectiveness of international efforts to contain them.
questions.planHtml:
Introduction — Thesis

Germany and Japan reached the same destination — full-scale war justified by ideologies of racial or national destiny — by different institutional routes: one driven by a single dictator testing the limits of Western tolerance step by step, the other by a military establishment that had already escaped civilian control. What unites them is that international efforts to contain either were structurally incapable of imposing real costs before war began, which is why both expansions accelerated rather than slowed across the 1930s.

Body Paragraph 1 — Germany's ambitions

Hitler's expansion was incremental and carefully tested, each step calibrated to see how far Britain and France would allow revision to go before acting. The remilitarisation of the Rhineland in March 1936, involving only around 30,000 troops, went entirely unopposed despite breaching Versailles outright; the Anschluss with Austria (March 1938) and the Sudetenland/Munich Agreement (September 1938) then added territory and population without triggering war, confirming to Hitler that the pattern would hold.

Body Paragraph 2 — Japan's ambitions

Japan's path differed in one crucial respect: expansion was driven by the military acting largely independently of, and sometimes despite, civilian government. The invasion of Manchuria in 1931 proceeded without formal authorisation and was followed by full-scale war with China from July 1937, including the Nanjing massacre later that year. This was framed, much as German expansion was, as a civilising and resource mission — the "Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere" — giving both empires an ideological cover for what was fundamentally a resource and territorial grab.

Body Paragraph 3 — international response

In both cases, collective security produced condemnation without consequence. The League's Lytton Report of 1932 formally condemned Japan's actions in Manchuria but recommended no binding sanctions, and Japan simply withdrew from the League rather than comply. Britain and France's appeasement of Germany at Munich followed an identical logic to the West's response to Japan in China: protest registered, but no material cost imposed on the aggressor.

Conclusion — Judgement

The comparison shows collective security failed for structural reasons common to both theatres — no enforcement mechanism, no US participation, and a shared Western reluctance to risk war — rather than through any single diplomatic misjudgement specific to either Germany or Japan. That structural failure, replicated in two separate regions simultaneously, is what allowed both wars to begin within years of each other.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the circumstances that led to the formation of the United Nations in 1945.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Recognition that the League of Nations had failed to prevent a second world war, driven partly by its lack of enforcement power and the absence of major powers such as the USA.
  • Wartime Allied planning — the 1941 Atlantic Charter (Churchill and Roosevelt) and the 1944 Dumbarton Oaks proposals laid the groundwork for a new organisation with real enforcement power.
  • The UN Charter was signed in San Francisco by 50 founding members on 26 June 1945 and came into force on 24 October 1945, creating a Security Council with the power to authorise binding action — a direct attempt to fix the League's central structural weakness.
